text: Approach Site Suitability: Random Forest Approach • Existing data center locations are used to learn patterns for siting. • We use machine learning in two ways: ◦ Identify grid cells that have similar/comparable qualities to current buildout. ◦ Identify relative importance of different features for current buildout. • The problem of learning from existing data center locations is framed as a positive unlabeled learning problem. ◦ Positive unlabeled learning is a branch of semisupervised machine learning that deals with situations in which only positive labels are known (i.e., existing data center locations) but negative labels do not exist; hence, the rest of the dataset is “unlabeled” and could contain both positive and negative instances. ◦ A random forest with a non-negative risk estimator algorithm is applied on the data (Wilton et al. 2022). Site Suitability: Random Forest Approach • To define the data inputs to the model, a grid is defined over contiguous United States, and variables are characterized and normalized using reVeal. • Grid cells, which intersect data center locations, are labeled as positive instances. • The Baxtel dataset of data center locations is divided into operational, construction, and planned data center locations, and these are used to define training, validation, and testing datasets, respectively. • The validation dataset was used to tune the model hyperparameters.
